passages.original: Ergo ex futuris prisca coepit fabula, Factoque primo res notata est ultima, It ille mortis inchoator rusticus 497 Insulsa terræ deferens libamina, Deumque rerum1 mortuarum deputans, HasTis redacta digna sacris crederet, Viventis atrox armulator hostiæ. Agnosco nempe, quem figura hæcdenotet, Quis fratricida, quis peremptor invidus Prave sacrorum disciplinam dividat, Mactare dum se vota censet rectius. Marcion, arvj forma corruptissimi, Docet, Duitas discrepare a spiritu, 498 Contaminatæ dona carnis offerens, Et segregatim numen æternum colens. Qui si quiescat, nec monentem negligat, Pacem quietam diligat germanitas, Unum, atque vivum fassa vivorum Deum.
passages.english: So the ancient story began from things to come, and in the first deed the last event was signalled. That rustic starter of death goes forth, bringing tasteless offerings of the earth, and, reckoning God to be a God of dead things, he supposed that things reduced to dust were worthy of the rites, a savage rival of the living victim. I recognise, surely, whom this figure denotes: who is the fratricide, who the envious slayer who wrongly divides the discipline of the sacred rites, while he thinks he sacrifices his vows more rightly. Marcion, the image of that most corrupt [man] of the field, teaches that two deities differ from the Spirit, offering the gifts of defiled flesh and worshipping the eternal godhead separately. If he would keep quiet, and not neglect the one who warns him, brotherhood would love a quiet peace, confessing one and living God of the living.
passages.notes: The figure is Cain ("rustic", tiller of the field), as the context makes clear. "arvj" read as "arvi" (of the field); "Duitas" read as "duas" or "deitates" (two deities), uncertain. "HasTis" read as "Has tis"/"has cineris"?: rendered with "redacta" as "things reduced [to dust]"; the line seems corrupt and the rendering is tentative. "rerum1" and "hæcdenotet" corrected silently. The numbers 497 and 498 are line numbers and have been omitted.

passages.original: 538 Angulus hic portae in capite est: hic [continet omnem Saxorum seriem, constructaque limina firmat : Quem qui rite suis per propugnacula muris Noverit insertum, seque, ac sua moenia vallo Praecingat triplici, celsa stans eminus arce, Fretus amore petræ, castis et pervigit armis: Non illum regina Tyri, non accola magni Euphratis Parthus rapicl, non decolor Indus , Tempora pennatis redimitus nigra sagiuis. Quin, si fulmineos cogens ad bell a gigantas Allophylus tua castra velit delere tyrannus, Tutus eris : nec te firmo statione movebit Ipse Charon mundi, numen Marcionis: ipse Qui regit aerio vanas sub sole tenebras. 539 Nam vanum, quidquid sol aspicit: ex [elementis Cuncta solubilibus, fluxoque crcamine con- [stant. Fallo, creaturam nisi doctor Apostolus omnem Subjectam vanis non sponte laboribus orsus, Perjuro ingemuit miserans servire latroni.
passages.english: This is the corner at the head of the gate: it holds together the whole course of stones and makes firm the built threshold. Whoever duly knows it to be set into his walls along the ramparts, and girds himself and his fortifications with a triple rampart, standing far off on a lofty citadel, trusting in love of the rock, and keeps watch in chaste arms: him neither the queen of Tyre, nor the Parthian who dwells by the great Euphrates, nor the dark-skinned Indian, his black temples wreathed with feathered arrows, will carry off. Indeed, if a foreign tyrant, gathering thunderbolt-hurling giants to war, should wish to destroy your camp, you will be safe: nor will Charon of the world himself, the god of Marcion, move you from your firm post, he who rules the empty darkness beneath the airy sun. For whatever the sun looks upon is empty: all things consist of elements that dissolve and of a fluid substance. I am mistaken, unless the teacher, the Apostle, having begun [to speak of] the whole creation subjected unwillingly to empty labours, groaned in pity that it serves a perjured robber.
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: "rapicl" = rapiet, "sagiuis" = sagittis, "bell a" = bella, "crcamine" = cremine (rare word, apparently 'substance/mass'; reading uncertain), "pervigit" = pervigil. Numbers 538, 539 are line numbers, omitted. "Charon mundi" for Marcion's god as a lord of death is so in the text; the image of the corner-stone refers to Christ.
